strengths: Timely and well-motivated benchmark: CityLens addresses a genuine gap—no prior benchmark systematically evaluates LLVMs on urban socioeconomic prediction with both street view and satellite imagery.
Broad coverage: 17 cities across 6 continents, 11 indicators across 6 socioeconomic domains, and 17 LLVMs (open-source and proprietary), giving reasonable diversity of models, regions, and tasks.

Thoughtful benchmark construction methodology: perceptual-relevance filtering and Pearson-correlation-based redundancy removal for indicator selection are sensible and documented (28 -> 11 indicators, with full source list in appendix).

Useful empirical analyses: city-level performance variation (GDP task), ablation of satellite imagery impact, effect of street view image count, and task-level comparison of Direct vs. Normalized estimation yield interpretable insights (e.g., models collapse toward city averages; feature-based regression outperforms direct prediction).
Prompt templates and case studies (refusals, per-model outputs) are provided in the appendix, aiding reproducibility; code and data are stated to be open-sourced.
weaknesses: Missing baselines critically weaken the evaluation: no comparison against existing supervised or classical methods (e.g., contrastive-learning approaches [14, 23, 27], UrbanCLIP/UrbanVLP, or even a GeoLLM coordinate-only baseline with images absent). Without these, it is impossible to judge whether the observed LLVM performance (mean R² ~0.25-0.34) is weak relative to what is achievable, or whether the benchmark itself is the bottleneck.

The comparison across the three paradigms is unfair and partly undermines the headline conclusion: Feature-Based Regression uses a trained LASSO regressor while Direct/Normalized prediction are zero-shot, yet the paper concludes feature-based methods 'significantly outperform.' The authors acknowledge this, but the claim is repeated as a main finding without a like-for-like control (e.g., fine-tuned or few-shot predictor variants).

The filtering rule in Section 3.3.1 (excluding data points where either R² <= 0.5) discards most of the results and biases the Direct-vs-Normalized analysis toward tasks that already work; the resulting 'task preference' conclusions rest on a small, non-random subset and lack statistical support.

No significance testing, error bars, or multiple-run variance for model outputs (sampling temperature, prompt sensitivity), and no human performance ceiling, so results in Table 1 are hard to interpret; nRMSE results are promised as a metric but largely absent from the main results.

Data-quality and contamination concerns are unaddressed: many ground-truth sources (Zillow, WorldPop, GDP grids, Wikipedia-derived knowledge) may appear in model pretraining corpora; there is no decontamination discussion or test of whether models recall rather than perceive. Label alignment for global tasks (randomly sampled satellite tiles paired with 1km-resolution GDP/population values) introduces spatial coarseness/misalignment that is not quantified.

Internal inconsistencies and presentation issues: conflicting city counts (14 cities represented vs. 13 evaluated in the GDP analysis), indicator counts that don't reconcile cleanly across Sections 2.1.1, Table 2, and Figure 3, typos ('leisre', broken URL in the abstract, malformed reference [1]), and low-legibility figures (Figure 4, Figure 5a).

Scope of conclusions is limited: the dominant finding—that LLVMs are currently poor at this task—provides limited actionable signal, and the paper offers mostly speculative explanations for observed patterns (e.g., why Gemma3-12B beats 27B) without supporting experiments.

strengths: Timely and reasonably well-motivated problem: systematically evaluating whether large vision-language models can perform urban socioeconomic sensing is an interesting question, and the paper claims to be the first unified benchmark for this with both street view and satellite imagery.

Broad empirical coverage: 17 globally distributed cities, 11 indicators across 6 domains, 17 LLVMs, and three evaluation paradigms (Direct Prediction, Normalized Estimation, Feature-Based Regression), which is a substantial amount of evaluation effort.
Useful ablation-style analyses are included: the effect of the number of street view images, the (surprising) marginal contribution of satellite imagery, and city-level performance variation.
Dataset construction is documented in reasonable detail, including sources for 28 indicators (Table 2), definitions of transport indicators, and example prompts in the appendix.
weaknesses: Unfair and misleading comparison across paradigms: the headline finding that Feature-Based Regression 'significantly outperforms' Direct/Normalized prediction is not a like-for-like comparison — the former uses a trained LASSO regressor with 5-fold cross-validated supervision, while the latter are zero-shot. Presenting this as a capability gap of LLVMs overstates the conclusion, and the paper itself admits this in the Discussion but still frames it as a main result.

Suspicious data exclusion criterion: Section 3.3.1 excludes all data points where R² ≤ 0.5 'as such values generally reflect weak predictive performance and are not analytically meaningful.' This post-hoc filtering selectively removes exactly the (majority of) results showing models fail, biasing the reported comparison; it also contradicts the surrounding text, which reports House Price scores around 0.2.

No classical/learned baselines: the benchmark claims to quantify LLVM limitations, but there is no comparison against specialized contrastive-learning or CV-feature baselines (e.g., the UrbanVLP-style or Fan et al. [14] pipelines the paper cites). Without these, it is impossible to know the achievable headroom on the benchmark or whether the tasks are simply too noisy to be predicted from imagery at all.

Questionable ground-truth quality and task validity: GDP and population are derived from gridded global model products at 1 km resolution (themselves estimated data), house prices are ZIP-level Zillow values spatially overlaid onto census tracts, and several indicators (e.g., crime counts, GDP of a satellite tile) have weak visual grounding. High label noise likely deflates all R² values, making 'models fail' conclusions partially an artifact of noisy targets rather than model limitations.

Indicator selection is ad hoc: dropping obesity but keeping mental health because of a correlation (r=0.75) is arbitrary — high correlation argues the pair is redundant but not which one to keep — and the causal justification ('people under stress overeat') is unsupported speculation. Similarly, 'perceptual relevance' filtering is asserted without any human validation experiment.

No statistical rigor: R² values are reported as point estimates without confidence intervals, significance tests, or multiple seeds; some tasks have very small samples (193, 389 cases), where R² is notoriously unstable. Differences between models (e.g., Gemma3-12B vs 27B, 'relative drops of 4.3% and 6.8%') are interpreted as meaningful without any uncertainty quantification.

Normalization design is under-specified and arbitrary: mapping all indicators to a 0.0–9.9 scale with one decimal place lacks calibration detail (how are scale endpoints defined per indicator? consistent across cities with very different distributions?), making the Normalized Estimation results hard to interpret or reproduce.

Internal inconsistencies and sloppiness: Section 3.4.1 states '14 cities' then 'Among the 13 cities evaluated' for the same experiment; Figure 5a contains an unexplained R² of -0.61; typos ('leisre-time'); inconsistent terminology (LLVM/LLM/VLM used interchangeably); the abstract's open-source link is empty; Figure 3's sample counts (e.g., 1135 vs 1138) do not reconcile with the stated sampling caps.

Novelty is overstated: the paper claims to be 'the first benchmark' for LLVM-based socioeconomic sensing, but closely related works [24], [28], [46] already evaluate LLMs/VLMs on socioeconomic prediction across granularities; the delta is primarily more cities/indicators, which is incremental rather than a new research insight.

Findings are largely anecdotal: key claims (satellite imagery adds nothing, model scale doesn't help) rest on single model–task combinations (Gemini-2.0-Flash on 3 tasks; Llama4-Maverick on House Price) rather than systematic sweeps, weakening generalizability.

Ethical treatment is inadequate: predicting crime, poverty, and health status of specific neighborhoods from imagery raises significant fairness, privacy, and misuse concerns (surveillance, discriminatory applications, geographic bias), yet the paper contains essentially no ethics discussion beyond prompting the models to act as 'professional data analysts.'

Clarity issues in the core methodology sections (2.1.4 task construction mixes three different regional units and sampling schemes in dense prose), and the 'Discussion' appears as Section 6 after the Conclusion, suggesting an unpolished draft.

strengths: Fills a genuine gap: there is currently no unified benchmark that systematically evaluates large vision-language models on urban socioeconomic sensing with both satellite and street view imagery; the positioning against prior work (UrbanCLIP, UrbanVLP, GeoLLM, CityBench, UrBench) is well argued.

The benchmark construction is substantial and thoughtful: 17 cities across 6 continents, 28 candidate indicators filtered down to 11 tasks via explicit perceptual-relevance and redundancy-reduction criteria (Pearson correlation analysis), with clearly documented data sources in the appendix.

The three evaluation paradigms (Direct Metric Prediction, Normalized Metric Estimation, Feature-Based Regression) are well motivated and allow the authors to disentangle different failure modes (numerical grounding vs. visual feature extraction), and the analysis of which tasks favor which paradigm is a useful empirical insight.

Broad model coverage: 17 recent open-source and proprietary LLVMs of varying scales, enabling meaningful cross-model and cross-scale comparisons (e.g., the Gemma3 vs. Qwen2.5VL and scaling-trend analyses).

Detailed ablation-style analyses (city-level variation, satellite image impact, street view image quantity) and honest reporting of near-zero/negative R2 scores, with a transparent discussion section that does not oversell current model capabilities.
Detailed prompts, indicator definitions, and data source documentation in the appendix support reproducibility of the evaluation protocol.
weaknesses: No classical baselines: the paper criticizes prior deep learning approaches ([14], [23], [27]) but never compares LLVMs against them on the same data. Without a trained CNN/contrastive-learning baseline (e.g., the very method from [14] whose feature taxonomy the paper reuses), it is impossible to judge whether LLVMs add value over established approaches, which weakens the significance of the 'models still exhibit limitations' conclusion.

Methodological novelty is limited: the benchmark largely assembles existing data sources and reuses the visual taxonomy and evaluation design of [14] and GeoLLM [29]; the contribution is mainly a large-scale evaluation study rather than new technique or insight beyond 'models perform poorly'.

Potentially problematic analysis choice: in Section 3.3.1 data points where R2 <= 0.5 are excluded before visualization 'as such values generally reflect weak predictive performance and are not analytically meaningful.' This post-hoc filtering of uninformative results can bias the Direct vs. Normalized comparison and is not clearly justified.

Internal inconsistencies in the reported statistics: e.g., the abstract/intro claim 17 cities, but the city-level analysis (Fig. 5a) alternately mentions 14 and 13 cities; Table 1 caption and figure captions contain mismatches (Fig. 3a/b labels appear swapped); typos ('leisre-time', 'Indicator Souce') and an empty open-source link ('open-sourced via .') undermine polish and reproducibility claims.

The Feature-Based Regression paradigm uses a trained LASSO regressor while the other two paradigms are zero-shot; the headline claim that feature-based regression 'significantly outperforms' the predictors conflates evaluation setting with capability, and the authors' own discussion acknowledges this unfair comparison without resolving it.

Uneven experimental coverage in the detailed analyses: the satellite-image ablation uses only Gemini-2.0-Flash on 3 tasks, the image-quantity study only Llama4-Maverick on one task, and the city-level study only Gemma3-12B on one task; generalizing from these single-model, single-task experiments to benchmark-wide conclusions is weakly supported.

Sampling decisions raise fairness and coverage concerns: up to 500/1000 randomly sampled cases per task, random geographic point sampling for global tasks, and different image sources (Baidu vs. Google Street View) could confound cross-region comparisons; potential data-quality and licensing issues (scraped Lianjia housing data) are not discussed.

The claim of being the 'first benchmark' in this space should be tempered given closely related concurrent efforts (e.g., [24], [46] evaluating LLMs/VLMs on socioeconomic tasks), and the writing/terminology ('LLVM') is non-standard and inconsistent with the broader literature ('VLM'/'MLLM').

strengths: The paper presents the most extensive benchmark to date for evaluating LVLMs on urban socioeconomic sensing, spanning 17 globally distributed cities, 11 indicators across 6 domains, and 17 models — a clear resource contribution with broad geographic and modal coverage.

The evaluation design covers three distinct paradigms (Direct Metric Prediction, Normalized Estimation, Feature-Based Regression), enabling analysis of how task formulation interacts with indicator semantics, which is a genuinely interesting angle.

The experimental scope is unusually thorough for a benchmark paper: CoT vs. standard prompting, reasoning models, vision encoder ablations, street view image quantity and modality ablations, city-level analysis, nonlinear regressors, fine-tuning upper bounds, an error analysis, and a bias audit for Global North vs. Global South cities.

Reproducibility is taken seriously: an open-source Mapillary variant of the dataset is provided alongside the Google/Baidu version (with pano IDs and download scripts), and code is released; the ethics statement addresses privacy, geographic bias, and misuse reasonably well.

Several findings are actionable, e.g., that street view imagery dominates satellite imagery for these tasks, that feature-based regression outperforms direct prediction, and that fine-tuned LVLMs dramatically outperform zero-shot models.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the dataset is largely assembled from pre-existing public sources (Zillow, WorldPop, PLACES, SafeGraph, Lianjia, etc.) and the three evaluation paradigms are adapted from prior work (Fan et al., 2023; Manvi et al., 2024b). The core contribution is breadth of aggregation rather than a new method or insight.

The headline comparison is unfair and potentially misleading: Feature-Based Regression uses a trained LASSO regressor with supervised labels, while Direct/Normalized settings are zero-shot. The paper's conclusion that LVLMs are 'better as feature extractors than predictors' is partly an artifact of this design asymmetry, as acknowledged only in the appendix.

Excluding model-task pairs with R^2 <= -0.5 (Section 3.2) is an ad hoc filtering rule that makes cross-setting comparisons non-comparable and selectively removes the worst failures, weakening the Direct vs. Normalized analysis.

Some central results are confirmatory rather than surprising: visually grounded indicators (building height, public transport) are easier to predict than latent ones (mental health, life expectancy) — this was predictable from the indicator selection criterion (perceptual relevance) itself, partially circularizing the analysis.

Several tasks appear inherently ill-posed at the chosen granularity (e.g., predicting per-census-tract GDP or life expectancy from 10 street views), so near-zero R^2 results may say little about LVLM capability; the paper does not establish a meaningful human-expert baseline despite mentioning 'Human Test' only in indicator selection.

Ground-truth quality concerns are underexplored: ZIP-to-census-tract averaging for house prices, 1 km-resolution GDP tiles, and gridded population products introduce label noise that caps achievable R^2, yet no label-noise analysis or error decomposition is provided.

Fine-tuning results (Table 2) risk train/test distribution overlap: models are fine-tuned on 'additional CityLens data' for the same tasks/regions, and no attempt is made to quantify contamination or leakage between training and benchmark regions.

Small task sample sizes (e.g., 193 regions for Life Expectancy, 389 for Violent Crime) and lack of confidence intervals or significance tests make many model-to-model differences (e.g., the claimed 4.3% and 6.8% relative drops between Gemma3-12B and 27B) statistically unsupported.

Presentation issues undermine polish: the abstract's code/data link is empty ('available at .'), the reproducibility section lists two blank URLs, and there are multiple typos ('leisre-time', 'Misuse Declaimer', 'along geographic coverage').

strengths: Large-scale benchmark construction: 17 cities across 6 continents, 11 indicators spanning 6 domains, 17 LVLMs, and 3 evaluation paradigms, which is genuinely broader in geographic and indicator coverage than prior urban socioeconomic benchmarks.

Thorough evaluation methodology: comparing direct prediction, normalized estimation, and feature-based regression is a sensible design, and the paper includes many useful ablations (input modality, number of street view images, CoT prompting, reasoning models, vision encoder backbones, nonlinear regressors, city-level analysis, and a bias audit).

Good reproducibility practices: an open-source Mapillary version of the dataset, pano-id lists plus download scripts for the API-based version, released code, and detailed appendix documentation of data sources and aggregation strategies.

Useful empirical findings: feature-based regression outperforming direct/normalized prediction, street view imagery being more informative than satellite imagery at this resolution, performance gaps between Global North and Global South cities, and fine-tuned LVLM results suggesting a higher achievable upper bound.
Reasonably strong ethics statement addressing privacy, geographic bias, and misuse, with an explicit disclaimer that the benchmark should not inform real-world policy decisions.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the paper is primarily a data-collection and evaluation exercise whose headline findings (visually grounded tasks are easier; fine-tuning helps; feature extraction is easier than precise numeric prediction) are largely confirmatory and unsurprising. The insights do not substantially advance understanding beyond existing work (e.g., UrbanVLP, GeoLLM).

Claimed human test is missing: the indicator selection pipeline (Figure 2) states that a 'Human Test' is used to assess perceptual relevance, but no human performance results are reported anywhere. A human baseline is essential to calibrate task difficulty and to support the claim that low R2 reflects LVLM limitation rather than task impossibility.

Evaluation rigor concerns: no statistical significance testing, no confidence intervals, or multiple runs are reported; R2 on small samples (e.g., Life Expectancy with only 193 MSOAs) is highly unstable, and 'relative improvements' of 6.4%-255% computed on R2 values are a questionable metric.

Inconsistent exclusion policy: in the Direct/Normalized comparison, model-task pairs with R2 <= -0.5 are excluded and model identity is abstracted away. This non-standard filtering can materially bias the comparison between the two paradigms and makes results hard to interpret or reproduce.

Potential confounding between visual grounding and parametric knowledge: prompts explicitly reveal the city and country, so models may exploit geographic priors rather than image content. The no-image baseline is only explored for one task (House Price), and the paper does not systematically separate visual signal from geospatial priors.

Internal inconsistencies: the abstract claims 17 globally distributed cities while the GDP task covers 13 cities; the abstract mentions 11 tasks/6 domains but Figure 1 image captions and dataset statistics (Table 3b) contain mismatched numbers and unclear task labels (e.g., house price caption shows a population question). These errors reduce confidence in the data pipeline.

Fine-tuning 'upper bound' claim is weakly supported: fine-tuned models are trained on data from the same cities and the same data distribution as the evaluation tasks, so the strong Table 2 results likely reflect distribution memorization rather than a realistic upper bound on generalization; cross-city or held-out-city evaluation is needed.

Writing and presentation quality is uneven: several grammatical issues ('Indicator Souce', 'Misuse Declaimer', 'no leisre-time'), a broken URL in the abstract, inconsistent figure captioning, and redundant prose suggest insufficient polish for a top-tier submission.

Negative results dominate (most R2 near zero or negative), yet the paper does not develop a rigorous diagnostic to explain failure; the error analysis is anecdotal (a few qualitative cases) and the 'hypotheses' in Appendix A.10 are speculative and unvalidated.

strengths: Comprehensive benchmark scope: CityLens covers 17 globally distributed cities, 11 socioeconomic indicators across 6 domains, 17 state-of-the-art LVLMs, and 3 distinct evaluation paradigms, making it the most extensive benchmark of its kind for urban socioeconomic sensing with LVLMs.

The evaluation methodology is thoughtfully designed: the three paradigms (Direct Metric Prediction, Normalized Estimation, Feature-Based Regression) probe complementary capabilities, and the analysis of which tasks benefit from which formulation (Figure 5, diagonal analysis) yields genuinely useful insights about task semantics vs. prediction strategy.

Extensive and well-structured experimental analysis: city-level variation, input modality ablations (street view vs. satellite), image quantity scaling, CoT vs. standard prompting, reasoning models, vision encoder comparisons, nonlinear regressors, and error case studies provide depth beyond a simple leaderboard.

Strong reproducibility commitment: the release of pano IDs plus download scripts for the proprietary street view version, a fully open Mapillary variant with parallel results (Appendix A.3), and full code release materially improves the practical utility of the benchmark.

Good empirical finding on street view vs. satellite contributions (Section 3.3), which contradicts prior assumptions and is useful for practitioners; fine-tuning experiments (Table 2) give a meaningful estimate of what adapted LVLMs can achieve, motivating the benchmark's purpose.

Ethics and fairness treatment is above average: privacy handling of street view imagery, misuse disclaimer, and a preliminary Global North/South bias audit (Appendix A.9) are included rather than omitted.
weaknesses: The headline finding—that LVLMs struggle to predict socioeconomic indicators, with most R² values low or near zero—may limit the benchmark's immediate utility; several conclusions (visual tasks are easier than latent ones; scale doesn't monotonically help) are somewhat expected and the paper's novelty is primarily aggregation rather than new insight or method.

Ground-truth label quality is uneven and weakly justified in places: GDP and population are derived from ~1 km gridded products averaged over satellite-image footprints, house prices are transferred from ZIP-code to census-tract via crosswalk averaging, and tasks like Life Expectancy have only 193 regions—label noise from these mappings could materially depress measured R² and is not quantified or bounded.

The Feature-Based Regression paradigm, which dominates the main results, is essentially a re-application of the 13-attribute visual taxonomy from Fan et al. (2023) with an LVLM as scorer plus LASSO; its comparison against end-to-end baselines (UrbanVLP, UrbanCLIP) is somewhat apples-to-oranges given the trained regressor vs. zero-shot predictor asymmetry, and the paper acknowledges this but does not fully resolve it.

The exclusion rule (discarding model-task pairs with R² ≤ -0.5 in Section 3.2) introduces an evaluation-selection concern; the rationale and sensitivity of results to this filter are not reported, and figures with model identity abstracted away reduce verifiability.

Indicator selection rationale (Pearson-correlation-based redundancy removal, e.g., dropping obesity because r=0.75 with mental health) is heuristic; the mutual-information or downstream-discriminability argument is not validated, and some included indicators (e.g., GDP at 1 km resolution) arguably lack perceptual relevance by the paper's own stated principle.

The fine-tuning 'upper bound' experiment (Table 2) uses held-out benchmark data but is evaluated on the same benchmark the fine-tuning data was drawn from, risking optimistic bias; a fully cross-city held-out evaluation would be more convincing.

Some presentational and rigor issues: the writing contains minor errors (e.g., 'leisre-time', 'Misuse Declaimer'), Figure 7(b)/(c) panels appear duplicated in parsing, and several analyses (CoT effects, vision encoder comparison) are run on only 3-4 models and 3-4 tasks, limiting generalizability of those conclusions.
